title: On the nature of freedom: whether it opposes necessity or only compulsion is a verbal or minor dispute
source_text: VI. Quod spectat autem naturam libertatis, ut clarum etiam est ex iis quae praecedentibus disputationibus exposita fuerunt, non minor est in utraque Schola sententiarum varietas. Et primo quidem abunde probavimus, tam in hac, quam in illa Schola non deesse qui doceant, aliis reclamantibus, libertatem arbitrii oppositam non esse necessitati simpliciter, sed coactioni tantum. Verum illud quoque manifestum fecimus, quae hic est controversia, aut mere verbalem esse, aut saltem non magni momenti. Etenim qui affirmant libertatem in genere opponi non necessitati, sed coactioni solum, diversae sententiae Theologis concedunt, ad libertatem non sufficere immunitatem a coactione; nec libertatem in ea proprie consistere; sed in eo quod agens liberum seipsum movet & seipsum agit, ratione quadam agenti intellectuali propria, quae nec in rebus inanimis, neque in brutis reperitur.
pass_a_gloss: But as regards the nature of liberty, as is also clear from those things which were set forth in the preceding disputations, there is no less variety of opinions in either School. And first indeed we have abundantly proved, that both in this, and in that School there are not wanting those who teach, others protesting, that liberty of choice is opposed not to necessity simply, but to compulsion only. But we made this also manifest, that the controversy which is here, is either merely verbal, or at least not of great moment. For those who affirm that liberty in general is opposed not to necessity, but to compulsion only, grant to the Theologians of a different opinion, that immunity from compulsion does not suffice for liberty; nor does liberty properly consist in it; but in this, that a free agent moves itself and acts itself, by a certain manner proper to an intellectual agent, which is found neither in inanimate things, nor in brutes.
pass_b_english: On the nature of freedom, as the earlier disputations also make clear, opinion varies no less in both schools. First, we showed at length that in each school some teach, against the protests of others, that freedom of choice is opposed not to necessity as such but only to compulsion.

We also showed that the dispute here is either a mere matter of words or at least of little weight. Those who say that freedom in general is opposed only to compulsion, not to necessity, concede to theologians of the other view that being free from compulsion is not enough for freedom and is not, properly, what freedom consists in. It consists rather in the free agent's moving and acting itself, in a way peculiar to an intelligent agent and found neither in lifeless things nor in animals.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
